\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\rho$ be real, let $f$ be a real-valued function on
the $n$-dimensional sign cube, and let $S$ be a set of coordinates. The Fourier
coefficient at $S$ of the noise operator applied to $f$ is $\rho^{|S|}\widehat f(S)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Odd part in the first coordinate]
\lean{FABL.firstCoordinateOddPart}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p250-b005}
\label{FABL.firstCoordinateOddPart}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.firstCoordinateSlice}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f:\{\pm1\}^{n+1}\to\mathbb R$. The odd part of $f$
in its first coordinate is the function on $\{\pm1\}^n$ given by $x\mapsto
\bigl(f(1,x)-f(-1,x)\bigr)/2$, where the first-coordinate slices are evaluated at $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Even part in the first coordinate]
\lean{FABL.firstCoordinateEvenPart}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p250-b005}
\label{FABL.firstCoordinateEvenPart}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.firstCoordinateSlice}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f:\{\pm1\}^{n+1}\to\mathbb R$. The even part of $f$
in its first coordinate is the function on $\{\pm1\}^n$ given by $x\mapsto
\bigl(f(1,x)+f(-1,x)\bigr)/2$, where the first-coordinate slices are evaluated at $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier coefficients of the odd slice]
\lean{FABL.fourierCoeff_firstCoordinateOddPart}
\label{FABL.fourierCoeff_firstCoordinateOddPart}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.firstCoordinateOddPart, FABL.firstCoordinateSlice, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierCoeff_insert_zero_tailFrequency, FABL.monomial, FABL.tailFrequency}
\difficulty{3}
Let $f$ be a real-valued function on the $(n+1)$-dimensional sign cube, and define its
odd part in the first coordinate by half the difference of its slices at
first-coordinate signs $+1$ and $-1$. For every subset $S$ of the remaining $n$
coordinates, the Fourier coefficient of this odd part at $S$ equals the Fourier
coefficient of $f$ at the set consisting of the first coordinate together with the
corresponding subset of the last $n$ coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier coefficients of the even slice]
\lean{FABL.fourierCoeff_firstCoordinateEvenPart}
\label{FABL.fourierCoeff_firstCoordinateEvenPart}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.firstCoordinateEvenPart, FABL.firstCoordinateSlice, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierCoeff_tailFrequency, FABL.monomial, FABL.tailFrequency}
\difficulty{3}
Let $f$ be a real-valued function on the $(n+1)$-dimensional sign cube, and define its
even part in the first coordinate by averaging its slices at first-coordinate signs $+1$
and $-1$. For every subset $S$ of the remaining $n$ coordinates, the Fourier coefficient
of this even part at $S$ equals the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at the corresponding
subset of the last $n$ coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier coefficient of a coordinate slice]
\lean{FABL.fourierCoeff_slice_eq_tail_add_sign_mul_insert}
\label{FABL.fourierCoeff_slice_eq_tail_add_sign_mul_insert}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.firstCoordinateSlice, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierCoeff_insert_zero_tailFrequency, FABL.fourierCoeff_tailFrequency, FABL.signValue, FABL.signValue_neg_one, FABL.signValue_one, FABL.tailFrequency}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f:\\{-1,1\\}^{n+1}\\to\\mathbb R$, let
$b\\in\\{-1,1\\}$, and let $S\\subseteq\\{1,\\ldots,n\\}$. Write
$S^+\\subseteq\\{1,\\ldots,n+1\\}$ for the set obtained by shifting every coordinate in
$S$ up by one. The Fourier coefficient of the slice of $f$ with first coordinate fixed
to $b$, at $S$, equals the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $S^+$ plus $b$ times its
coefficient at $S^+\\cup\\{1\\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Noise operator on a coordinate slice]
\lean{FABL.noiseOperator_firstCoordinateSlice}
\label{FABL.noiseOperator_firstCoordinateSlice}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.card_tailFrequency, FABL.firstCoordinateEvenPart, FABL.firstCoordinateOddPart, FABL.firstCoordinateSlice, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierCoeff_firstCoordinateEvenPart, FABL.fourierCoeff_firstCoordinateOddPart, FABL.fourierCoeff_noiseOperator, FABL.fourierCoeff_slice_eq_tail_add_sign_mul_insert, FABL.fourier_ext, FABL.monomial, FABL.noiseOperator, FABL.signValue, FABL.tailFrequency, FABL.zero_notMem_tailFrequency}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f\colon\{−1,1\}^{n+1}\to\mathbb R$, and let
$b\in\{−1,1\}$. For $x\in\{−1,1\}^n$, write $f_b(x)=f(b,x)$, and define
$f_{\mathrm{odd}}=(f_1-f_{-1})/2$ and $f_{\mathrm{even}}=(f_1+f_{-1})/2$. For every real
$\rho$, the restriction of the noise operator applied to $f$ at first coordinate $b$ is
the function $x\mapsto b\rho\,(T_\rho f_{\mathrm{odd}})(x)+(T_\rho
f_{\mathrm{even}})(x)$, where $T_\rho$ denotes the noise operator on the $n$-dimensional
sign cube.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[KKL noise root]
\lean{FABL.kklNoiseRoot}
\label{FABL.kklNoiseRoot}
\leanok
The KKL noise root is the nonnegative square root of $1/3$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Square of the noise root]
\lean{FABL.kklNoiseRoot_sq}
\label{FABL.kklNoiseRoot_sq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.kklNoiseRoot}
\difficulty{1}
The square of the nonnegative square root of $1/3$ is $1/3$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $d,e:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$ and
$f:\{-1,1\}^{n+1}\to\mathbb R$. Suppose that $f(b,x)=bd(x)+e(x)$ for every
$b\in\{-1,1\}$ and $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$. Let $A,B\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $0\le A$ and $0\le
B$, and suppose that $\mathbb E[d^4]\le A^2/9$ and $\mathbb E[e^4]\le B^2$, with
expectations uniform on the respective cubes. Then $\mathbb E[f^4]\le(A+B)^2$, with
expectation uniform on the $(n+1)$-dimensional cube.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{5}
For every natural number $n$ and every function $f:\{−1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$, let $T$ be
the Walsh noise operator that multiplies the coefficient indexed by
$S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ by $(1/\sqrt{3})^{|S|}$. Then
\[
\mathbb E_x[(Tf(x))^4]\leq \bigl(\mathbb E_x[f(x)^2]\bigr)^2,
\]
where both expectations are uniform over the sign cube.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourth moment bound for a product average]
\lean{FABL.expect_mul_fourth_le_expect_sq_cubed_mul_expect_fourth}
\label{FABL.expect_mul_fourth_le_expect_sq_cubed_mul_expect_fourth}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.expect_fourth_nonneg, FABL.expect_sq_nonneg}
\difficulty{6}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, and let $g,h$ be real-valued functions on the
$n$-dimensional sign cube. Suppose that $g(x)^3=g(x)$ and $g(x)^4=g(x)^2$ for every
point $x$. Then $(\mathbb E[gh])^4\le(\mathbb E[g^2])^3\mathbb E[h^4]$, where the
expectations are uniform averages over the cube.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cubic identity for the discrete derivative]
\lean{FABL.discreteDerivative_toReal_cube}
\label{FABL.discreteDerivative_toReal_cube}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.discreteDerivative, FABL.discreteDerivative_apply, FABL.setCoordinate}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f$ be a function from the $n$-dimensional sign cube to $\\{\pm1\}$, let $i$ be a
coordinate, and let $x$ be a point of the cube. The discrete derivative of the
real-valued version of $f$ in coordinate $i$ at $x$ has cube equal to itself.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourth power of the discrete derivative]
\lean{FABL.discreteDerivative_toReal_fourth}
\label{FABL.discreteDerivative_toReal_fourth}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.discreteDerivative, FABL.discreteDerivative_apply, FABL.setCoordinate}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f$ be a function from the $n$-dimensional sign cube to $\{\pm1\}$, let $i$ be a
coordinate, and let $x$ be a point of the cube. The fourth power of the discrete
derivative of the real-valued version of $f$ in coordinate $i$ at $x$ equals its square.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f:\\{−1,1\\}^n\\to\\{−1,1\\}$ be a Boolean
function. For each coordinate $i$, the square of the stable influence of its real-valued
version at parameter $1/3$ is at most the cube of its Boolean influence, where Boolean
influence is the uniform probability that flipping coordinate $i$ changes the value of
$f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Maximum coordinate influence]
\lean{FABL.maximumInfluence}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p017-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p097-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p265-b003
}
\label{FABL.maximumInfluence}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.booleanInfluence, FABL.booleanInfluence_eq_influence_toReal, FABL.influence_nonneg}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f:\{\pm1\}^n\to\{\pm1\}$. Its maximum influence is
the largest, over all coordinates, of the influence of that coordinate on $f$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity of maximum influence]
\lean{FABL.maximumInfluence_nonneg}
\label{FABL.maximumInfluence_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.maximumInfluence}
\difficulty{1}
For every Boolean function $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$ on a finite sign cube, its maximum
coordinate influence is nonnegative.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Influence bounded by maximum influence]
\lean{FABL.booleanInfluence_le_maximumInfluence}
\label{FABL.booleanInfluence_le_maximumInfluence}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.booleanInfluence, FABL.booleanInfluence_eq_influence_toReal, FABL.influence_nonneg, FABL.maximumInfluence}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f:\\{-1,1\\}^n\\to\\{\\pm1\\}$, and let $i$ be a
coordinate. The influence of coordinate $i$ is at most the maximum influence of $f$ over
all coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Attainment of maximum Boolean influence]
\lean{FABL.exists_booleanInfluence_eq_maximumInfluence}
\label{FABL.exists_booleanInfluence_eq_maximumInfluence}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.booleanInfluence, FABL.booleanInfluence_eq_influence_toReal, FABL.influence_nonneg, FABL.maximumInfluence}
\difficulty{4}
For a Boolean function on the sign cube with $n>0$ coordinates, some coordinate has
influence equal to the maximum influence among all coordinates.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Total influence and maximum influence]
\lean{FABL.totalInfluence_le_natCast_mul_maximumInfluence}
\label{FABL.totalInfluence_le_natCast_mul_maximumInfluence}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.booleanInfluence, FABL.booleanInfluence_eq_influence_toReal, FABL.booleanInfluence_le_maximumInfluence, FABL.influence, FABL.maximumInfluence, FABL.totalInfluence}
\difficulty{4}
For every Boolean function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional cube, its total influence,
computed using its real-valued sign representation, is at most $n$ times its maximum
coordinate influence.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f:\\{-1,1\\}^n\\to\\{-1,1\\}$ be a Boolean
function. The square of the total stable influence of its real-valued sign
representation at parameter $1/3$ is at most the maximum coordinate influence of $f$
times the square of the total influence of that sign representation.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{6}
Let $f$ be a Boolean function on the sign cube of dimension $n$, and suppose its
variance is positive. Then three times its variance, multiplied by
$(1/3)^{I/\operatorname{Var}(f)}$, is at most its total stable influence at parameter
$1/3$, where $I$ denotes its total influence.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Edge KKL lower bound]
\lean{FABL.edgeKKL}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p267-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p267-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p267-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p268-b001
}
\label{FABL.edgeKKL}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.maximumInfluence, FABL.three_mul_variance_mul_rpow_le_totalStableInfluence_one_third, FABL.totalInfluence, FABL.totalStableInfluence, FABL.totalStableInfluence_nonneg, FABL.totalStableInfluence_one_third_sq_le_maximum_mul_totalInfluence_sq, FABL.variance, FABL.variance_le_totalInfluence}
\difficulty{5}
Let $f$ be a Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube with positive variance.
If $I(f)$ is the sum of its coordinate influences, $V(f)$ its variance, and
$I_{\max}(f)$ its largest coordinate influence, then $9\cdot
9^{-I(f)/V(f)}/(I(f)/V(f))^2\leq I_{\max}(f)$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{7}
For every natural number $n$ and every Boolean function $f:\{−1,1\}^n\to\{−1,1\}$, its
variance under the uniform measure, multiplied by $\log(n)/(100n)$, is at most its
maximum coordinate influence.
\end{theorem}
